/.title: The laboratory
/.intro: Computing for science. A meeting place for scientific communities, from numerical methods to applications.
/.html:
Maison de la Simulation brings physicists, mathematicians, computer scientists and engineers together to advance research through computing. A joint laboratory of CEA, CNRS, Université Paris-Saclay and UVSQ, we develop methods, software and working practices for large scientific computing infrastructures.

Connecting science and computing

Our work spans numerical simulation, parallel software engineering, programming models, visualisation, artificial intelligence and quantum computing. This combination connects physical phenomena, numerical methods and their implementation on computing systems.

We help scientific communities make effective use of computing resources, build connections across disciplines and turn advances in computing into scientific progress.

Three complementary missions

01 / RESEARCH

Design and explore

Develop projects at the intersection of mathematics, algorithms, computer science and physical applications. The laboratory hosts collaborations of different durations around high-performance computing.

Research with SoC →
02 / EXPERTISE

Support scientific applications

Contribute expertise in parallel algorithms, development, optimisation, visualisation and post-processing to help teams build and use their simulation tools.

Expertise with SbC →
03 / TRAINING

Share knowledge

Train researchers and engineers to use large computing systems efficiently. University teaching and continuing education help sustain the computing community across the Saclay campus.

Explore training →

/science-of-computing/.title: Research — Science of Computing
/science-of-computing/.intro: Developing methods, libraries and software environments that help scientific applications make effective use of large-scale computing.
/science-of-computing/.html:
The science behind large-scale computing

The Science of Computing (SoC) team develops methods and tools that help scientific applications benefit from high-performance computing. Computer science, artificial intelligence and applied mathematics come together in five complementary research areas.

Team leader: Julien Bigot.

Our research is connected with the national scientific computing community through RT Calcul (formerly GDR Calcul) and GDR C4P. The team is also connected with the CEA “Calcul intensif” network. These links support exchanges on numerical methods, parallel computing, software and computing architectures.

Explore the applications supported by SbC ↗Browse our software ↗

Programming for heterogeneous architectures

Contact: Mathieu Lobet.

We investigate performance portability, particularly with Kokkos and SYCL, and emerging GPU, FPGA and Arm architectures. Our goal is to make it easier to develop scientific applications that perform well across supercomputers, while exploring energy efficiency and quantum computing.

The team contributes to Kokkos and DDC, a library used by GYSELA-X++ for tokamak plasma simulation. We also study FPGA implementations of molecular dynamics and hydrodynamics kernels, using tools such as Maxeler and oneAPI.

These activities are connected with NumPEx / Exa-Soft, including Task 1.1 on C++ code transformations and optimisation, the CExA project on GPU computing tools, and the application work package of the HQI initiative.

Keeping data analysis close to the simulation

Contact: Yushan Wang.

Large simulations require new approaches to I/O and analysis. With PDI and its plugins, we develop data handling that is decoupled from simulation code. Deisa connects MPI applications with distributed Dask processing to analyse results during computation.

The team supports the integration of these tools, in situ analytics and event detection, in collaboration with the AI and visualisation group. It has contributed to data handling in the astrophysics applications ARK-MHD and NOVA++.

Maison de la Simulation contributes to the leadership of Exa-DoST, the NumPEx project on exascale data software and tools, and its Work Package 3.

Analyse, compare and visualise

Contact: Martial Mancip.

We build tools to make sense of simulation results, either during execution or after data has been stored. Computer vision and supervised learning help detect events and structures and produce indicators of a simulation’s evolution.

TiledViz & VRWall supports the exploration of simulation ensembles. VisIt, ParaView and VMD complement our analysis and visualisation workflows. These approaches also address complex data from medicine and biology.

Making scientific software usable

Contact: Julien Bigot.

A library’s usefulness depends on more than its algorithms. Installation, packaging, continuous integration and deployment are essential to adoption. Our experience combines the perspectives of users, library developers and supercomputer administrators.

Collaboration with IDRIS covers the software environments of Jean Zay and regional resources such as the Moulon computing centre. Supporting applications also builds practical experience with containers, including Singularity on Adastra.

Established as a dedicated activity in 2023, this work draws on Spack and Guix-HPC. It is part of NumPEx, including Exa-DI Work Package 3 on packaging, deployment and continuous integration.

Connecting mathematics and architectures

Contact: Samuel Kokh.

The team develops mathematical analysis and numerical methods suited to supercomputers and large datasets, connecting theoretical foundations with the requirements of large-scale execution.

Research covers large linear systems, numerical methods for partial differential equations — including finite volume methods — and algorithms for machine learning and artificial intelligence.

Software for the community

Discrete domain computation

DDC

A header-only C++ library for multidimensional meshes. It provides containers based on C++23 mdspan, geometric iterators and type-safe indexing. Mesh semantics support both generic and specialised algorithms.

Explore the project ↗

In situ analytics

Deisa

Deisa connects MPI simulations with distributed Dask processing. Analysing data during computation reduces transfers and intermediate storage.

Explore the project ↗

Performance portability

Kokkos

The Kokkos ecosystem supports C++ applications across different hardware architectures using a shared code base. It is a Linux Foundation project and part of the High Performance Software Foundation.

Explore the project ↗

Data interface

PDI

PDI decouples applications from data handling libraries. Code annotations and an external specification organise parameter reading, initialisation, post-processing, output, visualisation, fault tolerance, logging, coupling and simulation ensembles.

Explore the project ↗

Collaborative visualisation

TiledViz & VRWall

A web application for organising and exploring sets of results. Metadata supports sorting and comparison on a workstation or an image wall.

Explore the project ↗

Computing workflows

YML

YML describes parallel applications using the YvetteML workflow language, independently of the underlying environment: grids, peer-to-peer systems or metacomputing.

Explore the project ↗

/science-by-computing/.title: Expertise — Science by Computing
/science-by-computing/.intro: Supporting scientific applications, from numerical methods to execution on supercomputers.
/science-by-computing/.html:
Building with scientific communities

The Science by Computing (SbC) team helps scientific communities develop simulation codes and analysis tools. Working alongside researchers, it adapts applications to supercomputer architectures, particularly exascale systems, and shares this expertise across disciplines.

Team leader: Charles Prouveur.

Life science

Contacts: Yves Vandenbrouck and Jean-Michel Batto.

Maison de la Simulation contributes to the computing infrastructure for large-scale genomic data analysis being developed through the CEA–CAD collaboration. Planned for deployment at the TGCC, it will support genomic research and data reanalysis for healthcare.

The project combines data-workflow orchestration, analysis software and HPC resources, with secure computing environments, controlled data access and a preference for open-source components.

CEA–CAD infrastructure project ↗About CAD ↗

Astrophysics — ARK2-MHD

Contact: Pascal Tremblin.

ARK2-MHD is an open-source magnetohydrodynamics code for large-scale simulation, including turbulent flows, magnetic fields and convective dynamos in stellar atmospheres.

Its second-order MUSCL–Hancock finite volume scheme combines Kokkos for portability across OpenMP, CUDA and HIP with MPI for distributed execution. I/O and in situ analysis tools support scaling to thousands of GPUs.

The work presented covers resolutions up to 4096³ and tests on AMD MI300, NVIDIA H100 and Intel Max 1550 GPUs.

ARK2-MHD source code ↗

Fusion plasmas — GYSELA-X++

Contact: Thomas Padioleau.

This work develops reusable gyrokinetic operators in modern C++, based on Kokkos, DDC and PDI. Separating physical and computational concerns makes the code easier to maintain and extend.

Support includes Python integration for in situ analysis, packaging from laptops to supercomputers, performance analysis and optimisation.

The GYSELA-X++ project ↗

Physical chemistry — deMon2k and MDFT

deMon2k · Contact: Karim Hasnaoui.

With the TheoSim group at ICP Orsay, Maison de la Simulation supports this density functional theory (DFT) package through debugging, optimisation, parallelisation and GPU porting. The work uses MPI, OpenMP and ScaLAPACK for scalability, and MPI, CUDA/HIP and MAGMA for multi-GPU execution. It also includes an OpenACC implementation of the Kohn–Sham matrix.

MDFT · Contacts: Riccardo Spezia and Jean-Marc Lude.

MDFT uses molecular density functional theory to calculate solvation properties of complex solutes while retaining information on solvent structure, at a lower cost than QM/MM approaches.

Physical developments address different solvents, thermodynamic properties and coupling with an electronic structure code to optimise molecules in their solvent. Computational developments rewrite the spherical harmonics and FFT kernel with Kokkos FFT for heterogeneous computing.

deMon2k ↗TheoSim group ↗MDFT ↗

Light–matter interaction — Smilei

Contact: Charles Prouveur.

Smilei is an open-source, collaborative Particle-In-Cell code written in C++. It supports studies ranging from relativistic laser–plasma interactions to astrophysics, with physical modules and geometries evolving alongside community needs.

Engineers at Maison de la Simulation contribute to the core code, GPU porting of its modules and their use on recent supercomputers.

The Smilei project ↗

Energy — AMITEX and canoP

AMITEX_FFTP · Contact: Yushan Wang.

This distributed Fortran solver uses FFTs to simulate nonlinear mechanical behaviour in heterogeneous materials represented by regular 3D images. It runs on workstations, clusters and large HPC infrastructures.

The collaboration addresses GPU porting of constitutive laws and of the solver, particularly 3D FFTs with pencil domain decomposition.

canoP · Contact: Pascal Tremblin.

This open-source computational fluid dynamics library uses p4est to adapt the mesh to the solution. Refinement and coarsening concentrate resources where gradients are steep.

Models cover single-phase and two-phase flows: monofluid, the five-equation bifluid5eq model and the seven-equation Baer–Nunziato bifluid7eq model. They address different flow regimes for energy applications.

AMITEX_FFTP ↗canoP documentation ↗

/tiledviz-2/.title: TiledViz & VRWall
/tiledviz-2/.intro: Compare, organise and share scientific results, from a browser to an image wall and mixed reality.
/tiledviz-2/.html:
Exploring large sets of results together

TiledViz & VRWall is a web-based tiled visualisation application developed by CEA and LISN. It enables collaborative comparison, organisation and exploration of simulation results, on site or remotely.

Metadata associated with each result supports sorting and analysis. Support is tailored to each scientific community, so interactions and tools match the questions being investigated.

Designed around scientific use cases

The laboratory helps teams identify what needs to be compared, select useful metadata and design interactions that make analysis easier.

VRWall: an image wall in space

For presentations, demonstrations and collaborative work, VRWall brings the image wall concept into mixed reality. A headset and dedicated GPUs display and manipulate large visual content without a physical screen.

TiledViz use cases and architecture ↗Discuss your project ↗

/tiledviz/.title: TiledViz: use cases & architecture
/tiledviz/.intro: Brain imaging, climate science and collaboration: turning an image wall into a scientific analysis tool.
/tiledviz/.html:
Comparing ensembles, not just individual images

Simulation produces sets of results that cannot be understood through a sequence of isolated figures alone. In climate science, astrophysics and brain imaging, analysis often requires comparing tens or hundreds of cases simultaneously.

TiledViz & VRWall retrieves results from a post-processing server and uses metadata to organise them. It supports sorting and grouping images, annotating thumbnails, selective zooming, moving rows and columns, and saving a layout for reuse.

Brain imaging: understanding cortical diversity

Patterns in cortical folds differ between individuals and emerge during development. Comparing them helps researchers study normal variability and anomalies associated with developmental conditions. NeuroSpin’s work includes building a dictionary of patterns from tens of thousands of brains.

This requires training datasets prepared and corrected by experts. Viewing many brains side by side, grouping similar conformations and synchronising their rotation supports this work and the validation of classification methods.

The BrainVISA platform, developed by NeuroSpin’s UNATI laboratory, provides cortical fold analysis tools. Its Anatomist visualisation software represents MRI data, brain meshes and sulci. Identifications can be corrected manually, while C++ and Python libraries support dedicated applications.

The BrainTwister prototype was developed with LRI at DIGITEO Moulon and Inria’s ExSitu team within DIGISCOPE. It demonstrated the value of image walls for NeuroSpin’s research and, in the longer term, the national CATI platform’s work on large cohorts.

From Wilder to Mandelbrot

BrainTwister used WildOS, a node-webkit platform developed at LRI by Michel Beaudouin-Lafon’s team. Multiple Anatomist instances displayed pairs of hemispheres on the Wilder wall, with approximately 100 million pixels across 6 metres.

Infrared interaction supported group selection and synchronised rotations, but moving elements between instances limited sorting. Freely comparing and rearranging brains is central to the scientists’ work.

At Maison de la Simulation, Mandelbrot provides 33 million pixels across 4.3 metres, with around twenty square metres of collaborative working space. The described setup uses a control workstation and tablets and differs from Wilder’s infrared and touch interaction systems.

An architecture for moving results

After WildOS and BrainTwister were installed at Saclay, TiledViz was designed as a generic application independent of WildOS, removing sorting constraints and supporting different families of simulations and experiments.

Visualisation applications run in Docker containers, exporting their output through VNC over secure tunnels. Sharing the host kernel and devices limits 3D rendering overhead. Containers also control communication ports and allow databases to be mounted read-only.

The described implementations include VNC communication on the cluster’s internal network and remote access through SSH tunnels. Early demonstrators ran up to a hundred containers on a shared-memory server, before distributing rendering across dedicated graphics nodes.

A client–server mechanism manages streams and launches remote containers as displayed elements move. Client startup is automated to maintain interaction across the full image wall.

Demonstrators in climate science and health

An initial prototype was built with LSCE and CliMAF work involving IPSL and Météo-France. It supported interactive sorting of climate output images using metadata, in a browser and during sessions in front of Mandelbrot.

Integrating Anatomist then enabled comparison of brain series from NeuroSpin databases. Both use cases share an objective: organise data visually so several specialists can examine it and discuss it together.

TiledViz and VRWall ↗Contact the visualisation team ↗

A client–server mechanism manages streams and launches remote containers as displayed elements move. Client startup is automated to maintain interaction across the full image wall. Demonstrators in climate science and health An initial prototype was built with LSCE and CliMAF work involving IPSL and Météo-France. It supported interactive sorting of climate output images using metadata, in a browser and during sessions in front of Mandelbrot. Integrating Anatomist then enabled comparison of brain series from NeuroSpin databases. Both use cases share an objective: organise data visually so several specialists can examine it and discuss it together. TiledViz and VRWall ↗ Contact the visualisation team ↗

/de-lassistance-a-lautonomie-limpact-de-.title: From assistance to autonomy: agentic AI in research
/de-lassistance-a-lautonomie-limpact-de-.intro: A day to examine agentic AI in science, its opportunities and limits, and the questions it raises for scientific quality, reproducibility and the organisation of public research.
/de-lassistance-a-lautonomie-limpact-de-.label: Scientific workshop

/job-m2-coupling-ia-for-hpc-internship/.title: MSc internship — AI and in situ analysis for thermal simulation
/job-m2-coupling-ia-for-hpc-internship/.intro: Detect events in a heat-equation simulation, build training datasets and integrate inference with Deisa. A six-month internship advertised for February 2024.
/job-m2-coupling-ia-for-hpc-internship/.label: Internship · archive

/job-phd-python-data-processing-on-super.title: PhD — Analysing parallel simulations with Python
/job-phd-python-data-processing-on-super.intro: How can data be analysed during simulation rather than transferred and stored? This NumPEx / Exa-DoST topic addresses co-scheduling simulation and distributed analysis with PDI, Deisa and Dask.
/job-phd-python-data-processing-on-super.label: PhD · archive

/job-postdoctoral-position-extension-of-.title: Postdoctoral position — AMITEX: non-periodic boundaries, GPUs and coupling
/job-postdoctoral-position-extension-of-.intro: A two-year project extending FFT-based material simulations through new boundary conditions, CPU/GPU architectures and coupling between local and global simulations.
/job-postdoctoral-position-extension-of-.label: Postdoctoral position · archive

/seminar-february-2019-hercules-🧑🏫-olivi.title: Hercules — Managing data from simulation codes
/seminar-february-2019-hercules-🧑🏫-olivi.intro: Olivier Bressand presents CEA-DAM’s data platform: parallel I/O, checkpointing and recovery, coupling and post-processing across different mesh and model families.
/seminar-february-2019-hercules-🧑🏫-olivi.label: Seminar · archive

/seminar-february-2019-mpc-the-multi-pro.title: MPC — A parallel runtime for multicore nodes
/seminar-february-2019-mpc-the-multi-pro.intro: Julien Jaeger presents MPC and the efficient combination of MPI, OpenMP and POSIX threads on large NUMA nodes.
/seminar-february-2019-mpc-the-multi-pro.label: Seminar · archive

/seminar-february-2019-padawan-🧑🏫-julien.title: PaDaWan — In-memory data exchange between applications
/seminar-february-2019-padawan-🧑🏫-julien.intro: Julien Capul introduces an in-transit infrastructure that intercepts simulation data to replace file-based exchanges while limiting changes to existing tools.
/seminar-february-2019-padawan-🧑🏫-julien.label: Seminar · archive

/seminar-january-2023-gestion-des-io-par.title: XIOS — Parallel I/O for climate simulation
/seminar-january-2023-gestion-des-io-par.intro: Yann Meurdesoif presents XIOS: XML descriptions, a Fortran API and I/O servers that write results in parallel with computation.
/seminar-january-2023-gestion-des-io-par.label: Seminar · archive

/seminar-march-2019-emulating-quantum-co.title: Emulating quantum computers to develop algorithms
/seminar-march-2019-emulating-quantum-co.intro: Victor Alessandrini presents a portable C++ library, its shared-memory, MPI and Python interfaces, and the role of emulation in quantum chemistry and teaching.
/seminar-march-2019-emulating-quantum-co.label: Seminar · archive

/seminar-march-2020-two-level-coarse-cor.title: Two-level Schwarz methods with PETSc
/seminar-march-2020-two-level-coarse-cor.intro: Serge Van Criekingen investigates coarse corrections and optimised transmission conditions for domain decomposition, with tests up to 16,384 CPU cores.
/seminar-march-2020-two-level-coarse-cor.label: Seminar · archive

/seminar-may-16-2023-development-and-gpu.title: YALES2 — Adaptive meshes and GPU porting for low-Mach flows
/seminar-may-16-2023-development-and-gpu.intro: Patrick Bégou and Vincent Moureau present dynamic tetrahedral mesh adaptation, projection methods and GPU porting efforts for YALES2.
/seminar-may-16-2023-development-and-gpu.label: Seminar · archive

/seminar-may-30-2023-denergium-🧑🏫-herve-.title: DENERGIUM — Improving the energy efficiency of computing infrastructures
/seminar-may-30-2023-denergium-🧑🏫-herve-.intro: Hervé Mathieu presents an approach combining energy measurements, models and AI to improve the use of HPC, AI and data-processing infrastructures.
/seminar-may-30-2023-denergium-🧑🏫-herve-.label: Seminar · archive

/seminar-october-24-2023/.title: Matching algorithms and architectures for inverse problems
/seminar-october-24-2023/.intro: Nicolas Gac examines GPU and FPGA acceleration for inverse methods: tomography, Bayesian approaches and SKA radio astronomy data processing.
/seminar-october-24-2023/.label: Seminar · archive

/simulations-numeriques-ab-initio-de-lir.title: Ab initio simulation of ionising radiation in matter
/simulations-numeriques-ab-initio-de-lir.intro: Aurélien de la Lande presents methods for tracking energy deposition in molecules, from electron dynamics to applications involving DNA, peptides and proteins.
/simulations-numeriques-ab-initio-de-lir.label: Seminar · archive

/software-optimization-for-petaflops-s-s.title: QMC=Chem — Scaling quantum Monte Carlo simulations to petaflops
/software-optimization-for-petaflops-s-s.intro: Anthony Scemama presents optimisation and parallelisation strategies for QMC=Chem and the electronic structure calculation of large systems.
/software-optimization-for-petaflops-s-s.label: Seminar · archive
